implementation_notes: JavaScript's enumeration message is the iteration protocol: an object is iterable when [Symbol.iterator]() returns an iterator whose next() yields { value, done }, and for...of drives that protocol, calling the iterator's return() to close it when the loop exits early. Built-ins (Array, String, Map, Set, TypedArray, NodeList) are iterable out of the box, while Array.prototype.forEach/map/filter/reduce provide the collection-side messages for arrays - forEach replacing a plain index loop where no break is needed. The classic index loop remains necessary for sparse-array holes, index arithmetic and performance-critical code because it avoids the iterator object and the callback call.
pitfalls: forEach cannot break and silently skips holes in sparse arrays; use for...of or a plain indexed loop when the walk must stop or every index must be visited.
return inside the callback returns from the callback only, and awaiting inside a synchronous forEach starts concurrent work instead of serialising the walk - use for await...of for async iterables.

Mutating the array during forEach/map changes what later callbacks see (removed elements are skipped, appended ones are never visited); for...of over a Mutating array has the same hazard for added elements.
